title: Event loop or threads?

rows.label: How waiting works
values: Sockets are non-blocking; the loop asks `epoll`, `kqueue` or IOCP which are ready and runs other callbacks meanwhile
The thread blocks in `read()` and the OS scheduler runs another thread

rows.label: Memory per connection
values: Just the state the callback needs, kept in heap objects
A whole stack: typically 8 MB of virtual address space on Linux with glibc, 1 MB reserved on Windows (a few KB for goroutines)

rows.label: Using many cores
values: One loop per core: Nginx runs a single-threaded worker per core; Redis users run several instances
Built in: threads run in parallel (except CPython with the GIL)

rows.label: CPU-bound work
values: Blocks every connection; hand it to a worker pool (`run_in_executor`, Node worker threads)
Fine: it runs on its own core while other threads carry on

rows.label: Shared state and locks
values: One callback runs at a time, so in-memory state needs no locks (but it can change across an `await`)
Any thread can touch shared memory at any moment: locks or atomics, with data races and deadlocks possible

rows.label: Typical failure
values: One slow callback (a big `JSON.parse`, a heavy regex, a synchronous file read) stalls every client
Deadlocks, races that appear only under load, and pool exhaustion when every thread waits on a slow dependency

rows.label: Debugging
values: Timing depends only on events, but logic is split across callbacks and stack traces stop at the loop (`async`/`await` helps)
Sequential code with real stack traces, but timing-dependent bugs are hard to reproduce

rows.label: Examples
values: Thread-pool servers in Java, C++ and Rust; Go goroutines and Java virtual threads as cheap threads

tip: If connections mostly wait on the network and there are thousands of them, an event loop is cheap and avoids locks. If the work is CPU-heavy, or the code and libraries are blocking, use threads, ideally from a pool. Goroutines and Java’s virtual threads blur the line: you write blocking, thread-per-request code, and the runtime parks a waiting thread and runs another on the same OS thread. Either way, keep slow work off the thread that serves everyone else.
